# Using the Appropriate Technology for Disaster Risk Mitigation: The Case of Extreme Heat Events

Md. Sahil Rafiqa , Arup Ratan Dasa , Mohammad Shakhawat Hosen Apurbaa , Nadim Reza Khandakera

a North South University

ABSTRACT This research initiative aims at alleviating high temperatures in corrugated iron sheds by coating them with locally available red oxide rust-proof paint and has yielded positive results. Impacted by higher seasonal temperatures due to global warming, Bangladesh faces challenges in cooling these sheds due to rural electric supply scarcity. Elevated temperatures inside the sheds lead to heat stress in poultry, resulting in increased mortality and reduced egg production. The research involves comparing heat transfer in painted and unpainted sheds, demonstrating the iron oxide coating to act as a heat transfer barrier. Field trials have revealed the painted shed to maintain temperatures 2°F-4°F lower throughout the day compared to the unpainted shed and to dissipate heat more gradually during cloud cover. This sustainable technique not only prevents rusting but also regulates temperatures in enclosed spaces, offering potential benefits for animal husbandry and human habitats such as slum housing. The method’s simplicity and sustainability make it advantageous for reducing human suffering during extreme weather, suggesting the importance of considering existing solutions rather than developing new ones.

The heat waves during April 2023 saw high mortality rate of poultry boiler chickens. The higher temperatures increase the indoor ambient temperature of corrugated iron roof sheds. It was reported that 30 chickens died of heat stroke in Belgacha union of Kurigram Sadar upazila. Similar accounts have been shared by other farmers in Harishwar Kaloa village in Sadar, mentioning that 15 chickens died in one farm due to heatstroke. Farmers highlighted that aside from heatstroke, the intense heat has induced diarrhea in broiler chickens, leading to distressing deaths (United News of Bangladesh, 2023.). With scarcity regarding the rural electric supply, air cooling and ventilation systems are not viable. High inside shed temperatures cause heat stress in the poultry, which then leads to higher mortality. Additionally, this also adversely effects egg production. To explore a sustainable remedy, a research initiative has been undertaken. This study involves applying an iron oxide rust-resistant coating to poultry sheds of similar sizes, subsequently comparing the heat transfer performance between the coated and uncoated sheds.

## Methodology

The research incorporates a combination of primary and secondary data. Initially, an extensive review of existing heat reduction strategies has been conducted through an analysis of the available literature. Subsequently, field surveys and interviews have been carried out with key personnel in the poultry industry to gather valuable insights. Following this, the study area located in Baupara, Gazipur within Greater Dhaka was chosen. This specific area was selected due to its significance for hosting over 500 farms, thereby serving as a representative location for the study. The roofs of two identically sized poultry sheds on the farm were subjected to different treatments: one had a coating of red iron-oxide paint, while the other served as the control and remained unpainted.

Both poultry sheds exhibit uniform dimensions, measuring 21 meters in length, 6.32 meters in width, and 3.08 meters in height. The corrugated iron sheets comprising the structure of both sheds are constructed from identical materials. These sheds are positioned adjacent to one another and are thereby subjected to identical climatic conditions. Additionally, both structures are equipped with identical ventilation systems. Both structures share a comparable overhead tree cover.

A controlled background experiment was carried out using six pieces of corrugated iron sheets, all having similar dimensions (25’’ x 17’’). Two iron sheets were allocated to each color (i.e., white and iron-oxide red) and two were kept in their manufactured conditions without any paint coating. Two samples of each color were chosen for more precise data and to rule out any anomalous values. Only the colors anticipated to have optimum reflective, heat transfer, and radiative properties in warm climates were chosen, one being white enamel paint and the other being iron-oxide paint. The painted and unpainted sheets were installed on a rooftop at the same angles for sunlight to fall directly on in order to assess their effectiveness at reducing heat.

An infrared thermometer was used to measure the temperature variations, and temperature readings were taken every 30 minutes from the upper surface in direct sunlight to observe the heat reflection or retention. After taking the upper surface reading, another reading was taken after 10 minutes to observe the heat transfer to the lower surface of the corrugated iron sheets. The experiment was conducted under different weather conditions.

This comparative setup aims to observe and analyze indoor temperature variations within the poultry farms. The study employs a hygro-thermometer to measure the ambient temperature variations within the sheds. Temperature measurements were gathered from both the edges and the central area of the poultry sheds, and the average temperature has been reported to ensure reproducibility. Different weather conditions, including hot summer days and monsoon weather, were deliberately chosen to encompass different environmental influences affecting temperature variations on the poultry farm.

Result and Discussions

The red rust-proof oxide paint that was used as a coating is typically composed of iron oxide as its primary constituent. Being a relatively poor conductor of heat, iron oxide serves to mitigate the transfer of heat from the metal surface to its interior. To mitigate and control the indoor temperatures, the roof coatings were applied as done in previous studies (Carrasco-Tenezaca et al., 2021; Peng et al., 2023).

The experiment was systematically replicated over three days (n = 3) during both summer and winter season. Summer trials were specifically carried out in April, as maximum temperatures are observed during this period. Conversely, winter experiments were conducted during the month of December. Temperature data sets were recorded from 10:30 a.m. to 6:30 p.m. in order to comprehensively assess the temperature fluctuations within the sheds.

The indoor ambient temperatures of the coated and uncoated poultry sheds were monitored between 10:30 a.m.-6:30 p.m., revealing a fluctuation in temperature as shown in Figure 2. Analysis indicates an average temperature decrease of roughly 2°F- 4°F during this period.

Even though the poultry shed coated in red rustproof paint had poor ventilation (see Figure 3) due to cloth coverings when compared to the uncoated shed, the overall ambient temperature was lower. The boundary of the chosen poultry sheds are bounded with nets and cloth covers as a method of ventilation and reducing temperature inside the poultry. In addition, ceiling fans are installed at various places inside the poultry sheds to prevent heat stress in poultry.

Thus, the implementation of proper ventilation can cause a further decrease in ambient temperature to be expected to be observed in the red rustproof-coated poultry shed. The ability to store heat for a prolonged period of time would be advantageous during the winter, thus reducing the need for add space heating.

The poultry industry, in Bangladesh plays a role in providing jobs to around six million people, with women making up 40% of the workforce. With an investment of over 300 billion Taka, this sector contributes 2% to the country’s GDP, as reported by the Bangladesh Poultry Industries Central Council (BPICC). Bangladesh is home to an estimated 65,000 to 70,000 poultry farms, and protecting and sustaining this industry from heat events is not only crucial for maintaining employment opportunities and a stable economy but also for ensuring a consistent supply of meat-based food. Additionally, energy shortages have posed challenges for ventilation systems on these farms. Hence, the proposed approach aims to support an area consisting of 500 farms by utilizing available materials that operate independently from energy sources for the effectively regulation of indoor temperatures. Carbon emissions come from the energy used for ventilation. Electric fans are setup inside the farm, which in term uses energy that leads to greenhouse gas emissions.

Increased temperatures have also had an adverse effect on human health, even resulting in deaths. This method can be applied to any housing consisting of tin-roofing to subdue indoor temperatures. In Bangladesh where approximately 84% of the population resides in homes with tin roofs, introducing an economical and sustainable method using locally sourced materials to reduce indoor temperatures in these tin-roofed houses would significantly benefit the people, considering the country’s vulnerability to extreme heat events. High temperatures leading to heatwaves and prolonged periods of elevated day and night temperatures impose cumulative physical stress on individuals, worsening major global causes of death (World Health Organization, 2018). This innovative technology diverges from conventional methods that rely on electricity and energy for ventilation and cooling. This shift is particularly significant, as rural communities and slums residing under tin shed roofs encounter energy shortages. This technology can also be implemented in the Rohingya and Geneva refugee camps. Increased indoor temperatures not only trigger public health crises but also bring about socioeconomic challenges such as reduced work capacity, lower labor productivity, restricted mobility, and increased poverty rates. This situation might exacerbate the situation, particularly in major urban centers such as Dhaka, Chittagong, and Rajshahi due to rapid urbanization, thus causing the Urban Heat Island Impact (Dewan et al., 2021). Hence, this mitigation measure of coating a roof with red iron-oxide could be a readily applicable, sustainable mitigation option for resource challenged economies.

## Conclusion

The conducted research emphasizes the significance of addressing extreme heat episodes in Bangladesh, particularly in poultry farms, by exploring a sustainable solution for mitigating indoor temperatures in sheds with corrugated iron roofs. The study has highlighted the adverse impacts of elevated temperatures on poultry health, resulting in increased mortality rates and decreased egg production and thereby exacerbating economic losses within the industry. Utilizing a locally available red oxide rustproof paint as a coating on the sheds has demonstrated promising outcomes at reducing indoor temperatures. The coated sheds experienced an average decrease of 2°F-4°F compared to unpainted sheds, showcasing the effectiveness of the iron-oxide coating as a heat transfer barrier. Beyond the poultry industry, this research offers broader implications for improving living conditions, especially for communities residing in tin-roofed houses across Bangladesh. The method’s simplicity and sustainability make it a viable option for combating extreme heat events by addressing challenges exacerbated by energy shortages and contributing to alleviating socioeconomic burdens. Moving forward, the application of the iron-oxide primer technique stands as a practical, cost-effective, and eco-friendly solution for regulating indoor temperatures in enclosed spaces. The study’s findings emphasize the urgent need to implement such interventions on a larger scale, accompanied by strategic policies and action plans to mitigate the adverse effects of heat stress on human health, livelihoods, and overall well-being in Bangladesh.

## Abstract

Chlamydomonas reinhardtii is a model green alga extensively used to study photosynthesis and cilia using molecular biology and genetics. Electroporation is a very common technique to integrate DNA into the nuclear genome, which is essential to generate mutant collections and express transgenes. Here, we describe a simple, fast, and efficient protocol to transform strains with an intact cell wall. The technique achieves good transformation efficiency without cell wall digestion or the use of commercial kits and is compatible with the widely available Gene Pulser electroporation system.

Key features

• High transformation efficiency of Chlamydomonas reinhardtii strains with an intact cell wall.

• Faster than currently available electroporation protocols.

Keywords: Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, Microalgae, Transformation, Electroporation, Cell wall

## Background

Chlamydomonas reinhardtii is a model green alga amenable to genetic engineering. Electroporation is a common technique to randomly integrate DNA into the nuclear genome through non-homologous end joining repair [1]. Several protocols have been developed, but they often require cell-wall-less strains, digestion of the cell wall, specialized electroporators (e.g., NEPA21, Nepagene) [2], or a commercial kit (i.e., MAX Efficiency Transformation Reagent for Algae kit, Invitrogen). Here, we describe a simple, fast, and efficient method to transform Chlamydomonas reinhardtii strains with an intact cell wall. Compared to previously published electroporation protocols by Crozet et al. [3,4] and Onishi and Pringle [5], we simplified the procedure by removing the cold incubation (20–30 min), allowing the electroporation part of our protocol (section C) to take approximately 30 min. We used a CHES pH 9.25 electroporation buffer [5], which has been reported to yield a high number of transformants and to be efficient with several transgenes and strains, including those with an intact cell wall [5–8]. Our protocol is suitable for the generation of randomly mutagenized mutant collections and transgenic approaches (e.g., complementation of mutants or protein localization) but not for the delivery of Cas9 ribonucleoprotein complexes.

## Procedure

A. Purification of the DNA cassette

1. Digest a sufficient quantity of plasmid DNA (typically 5–10 µg) with appropriate restriction enzymes (typically BbsI or BsaI for MoClo plasmids [3,9]) to isolate the desired cassette. If the size of the cassette is close to that of the vector backbone fragment, additionally cut the latter with another restriction enzyme to ensure good separation. It is also possible to linearize the plasmid without purifying the expression cassette on the gel [6].

2. Incubate the reaction for 3 h to overnight at 37 °C.

3. Separate the cassette by agarose gel electrophoresis and isolate it by gel purification.

4. Measure the DNA concentration with a NanoDrop spectrophotometer. Typical recovery yield is 60%–80%.

B. Chlamydomonas culture and harvesting

1. From this point on, all steps must be performed under sterile conditions, for example, in a laminar flow hood.

2. Inoculate Chlamydomonas reinhardtii culture in liquid TAP. Adjust the volume depending on the number of transformations; the minimum is 25 mL per transformation if cells are harvested at 2 × 106 cells/mL.

3. Incubate the culture at 25 °C with shaking (~120 rpm) and constant light (50–100 μmol photons m-2·s-1) until it reaches a concentration of 2–5 × 106 cells/mL, which takes 2–3 days. Cell concentration can be measured with a hemocytometer or a cell counter. Using optical density has not specifically been tested, but may be used following the methods developed in [12]. It is recommended to maintain the culture under 5 × 106 cells/mL by dilution when necessary. This protocol works with stationary phase cultures as well, but efficiency might be slightly reduced.

C. Electroporation and recovery

1. In 50 mL tubes, harvest 50 × 106 cells per transformation by centrifugation (2,500× g, room temperature, 5 min). Calculate the volume to harvest as follows: V = 5 × 107/concentration. For example, if the culture concentration is 2 × 106 cells/mL, the volume is V = 50 × 106/2 × 106 = 25 mL per transformation.

2. Remove all the supernatant and resuspend the cell pellet in CHES buffer to a final concentration of 2 × 108 cells/mL.

3. In a 4-mm-gapped electroporation cuvette, mix 250 μL of the cell suspension with 50–500 ng of the DNA cassette. 200 ng of DNA is usually sufficient, but the quantity may need to be adjusted depending on the expression cassette. Several samples can be prepared at the same time, as incubation time has little effect on the transformation efficiency.

4. Right before electroporation, gently flick the cuvette to resuspend the cells. If bubbles are present, tap the cuvette on the bench to eliminate them.

5. Proceed to the electroporation at 600 V, 25 µF, and 1,000 Ω. Electroporation also works with Bio-Rad systems that lack resistance control.

Note: The measured pulse time has been between 10 and 15 ms for successful transformations.

6. Transfer the cells to a 15 mL tube filled with approximately 10 mL of TS40 and rinse the cuvette twice with 500 μL of TS40 to recover all the cells.

7. Incubate the tubes at 25 °C and a light intensity of ~50 μmol photons m-2·s-1 horizontally on a rotary shaker at ~120 rpm (or in a tube rotator at moderate speed) for 12–16 h.

Note: Do not skip this recovery step, as it is essential for the cells to express the resistance gene.

D. Selection of transformants

1. Harvest cells by centrifugation (2,500× g, room temperature, 5 min).

2. Pour off almost all the supernatant, leaving a volume of ~300–500 μL.

3. Resuspend the cell pellet in the remaining liquid, spread on TAP agar plates supplemented with the relevant antibiotic, and dry.

4. Seal the plates with parafilm or breathable tape and incubate at 25 °C and 50–100 μmol photons m-2·s-1.

5. Colonies should appear after 4–6 days (Figure 1).

Problem: Low transformation efficiency.

Possible cause: Saturated or unhealthy culture.

Abstract  Mitigating rainfall-induced landslides requires an understanding of the failure mechanisms leading to their initiation. Evaluating how predicted failure mechanisms relate to the landscape’s topography, geomorphology, antecedent hydrological conditions, and other subsurface characteristics such as shear strengths and hydraulic properties is essential for identifying the factors that control landslide occurrence across the landscape. Most existing regional mechanistic models estimate outputs such as landslide area density or characteristics of individual landslides, but, to our knowledge, they do not distinguish between the underlying failure mechanisms that trigger these landslides. The objective of this study is to analyze the impact of various factors on the occurrence of different failure mechanisms across the topography. We present a novel mechanistic regional model that integrates a pseudothree-dimensional slope stability approach with the Parallel Integrated Hydrologic Model (ParFlow). The model, named CRISIS, predicts regional rainfall-induced landslides and classifies them into two distinct failure mechanisms: (1) a bottom-up saturation-induced failure caused by a rise of the groundwater table; and (2) top-down wetting-induced failure driven by either a downward propagating wetting front or the formation of a perched water table above less permeable subsurface layers. CRISIS was applied to a watershed in Utuado, Puerto Rico, that was affected by Hurricane Maria in 2017. It was first run with near-realistic conditions to provide best-estimate predictions of the observed landslides. It was then used in a series of hypothetical simulations with varied subsurface properties to investigate the conditions controlling different failure mechanisms. Results show that failure mechanisms were strongly controlled by geomorphic position and initial groundwater conditions. Bottom-up failures occurred mainly on steep hillslopes near valley bottoms, where initial groundwater tables were shallow, while top-down failures dominated steep slopes near ridge tops, where initial groundwater tables were deeper. Failure depth was primarily controlled by subsurface cohesion; shallower landslides occurred at lower cohesion values. Subsurface material type, defined by both shear strength and hydraulic properties, significantly affected the frequency, mechanism, and timing of failures. Notably, a sandy subsurface triggered the highest number of failures, all initiated by the bottom-up saturationinduced mechanism within a short timeframe.

Introduction Landslides continue to pose a major threat to both human lives and property in mountainous regions globally. Rainfall is a prominent trigger of landslides, accounting for approximately 90% of landsliderelated fatalities worldwide (Haque et al. 2016), although slope failures can also be caused by earthquakes or human-induced factors (Petley 2012; Wei et al. 2019). Rainfall-induced landslides are also part of climate change-related effects (Fang et al. 2025; Zhang et al. 2025). The expected increasing frequency and intensity of extreme precipitation events are likely to trigger more landslides annually (Haque et al. 2019). Patricola-DiRosario and Wehner (2018) concluded that human-induced climate change has significantly increased the rainfall intensity in major tropical cyclones, including Katrina, Irma, and Maria. Precipitation-induced landslides are also expected to increase amid evolving land use: deforestation, rapid urbanization, and unplanned development in landslide-prone areas (Haque et al. 2019). Assessing landslide susceptibility on a regional scale is crucial for informing policy decisions and ensuring effective planning for risk mitigation (Wu et al. 2025). Most existing rainfall-induced landslide mechanistic models focus on estimating the landslide area density (e.g., Malamud et al. 2004; Rossi et al. 2010), while more advanced models provide information on the potential failure’s location, size, geometry, and timing (e.g., Bellugi et al. 2015; Rana and Babu 2022). Although these outputs are valuable, understanding the failure mechanisms behind the landslides is also important to assess the realism of predictions. Rainfall-induced landslides are triggered by changes in the pore water pressures and seepage forces under fully or partially saturated conditions (Zhu and Anderson 1998; Gerscovich et al. 2006). The increase in the positive pore pressure, or the reduction in the matric suction within the vadose zone, decreases the effective stress, thereby decreasing the material’s shear strength and increasing the slope’s vulnerability to failure for a given strength (Iverson 2000; Collins and Znidarcic 2004). This is based on the generalized effective stress theory (e.g., Lu and Likos 2006), which builds upon Terzaghi’s effective stress principle (Terzaghi 1943), but integrates both saturated and unsaturated seepage conditions. Although a change in pore pressure within the soil profile is the underlying trigger in all cases, the specific failure mechanisms of rainfallinduced landslides vary depending on how water moves through the subsurface during a storm. In this context, a failure mechanism refers to the way instability is initiated and develops within a slope, whether it is triggered by elevated pore pressures that form near the ground surface and propagate downward (top-down wetting) or by pore pressures that develop at depth and migrate upward toward the surface (bottom-up saturation).

The dominant failure mechanism depends on a combination of factors, including the slope’s geomorphic position defined as the location on a specific landform (valley bottom, mid-slope, or ridge top), the subsurface shear strength and hydraulic properties, initial groundwater and antecedent moisture conditions, weathering profile, degree of bedrock fracturing (density, orientation, aperture), and storm temporal characteristics (such as intensity and duration). The interaction between the hydraulic properties of the subsurface and rainfall is also critical as this relationship governs the extent of water infiltration and, ultimately, the dominant failure mechanism (Kienzler 2007; Li et al. 2013). Depending on these conditions, alternative failure mechanisms may compete, with one eventually prevailing. Determining the failure mechanism is crucial as it affects the characteristics of the resulting landslide, including its area, volume, depth, timing, and runout distance (Onda et al. 2004; Katsura et al. 2008). The dominant failure mechanism largely governs the likely position of the potential slip surface, which in turn has a major impact on the volume of failing material and the landslide’s runout response (Springman et al. 2012). Bottom-up saturation-induced failure triggered by groundwater table rise (Fig. 1): This mechanism is accounted for in most existing models. Initially, the pre-existing groundwater table creates positive pore pressures below it that are insufficient to trigger failure, while the unsaturated zone above the water table maintains suction (negative pore pressures) that act as apparent cohesion, enhancing stability (Fig. 1a). With continued rainfall, infiltration and lateral subsurface flow from adjacent slopes raise the groundwater table, generating additional positive pore pressures beneath it. These elevated pressures reduce effective stress and the mobilized shear strength along a potential slip surface (Lambe and Whitman 1979; Collins and Znidarcic 2004; Hidayat et al. 2024). Once pore pressures become sufficiently high, failure occurs below the groundwater table (Fig. 1b). It is largely accepted that this mechanism may cause deep-seated landslides (Iverson and Major 1987; Ashland et al. 2006).

Top-down wetting-induced failure triggered by wetting front propagation (Fig. 2): In addition to failures in the fully saturated zone, slope failures can also be triggered within the vadose zone in partially saturated conditions (de Campos et al. 1992; Godt and Coe 2007). In this case, the initial groundwater table may be located at a significant depth below the ground surface, resulting in a thicker unsaturated zone with significant matric suction (Fig. 2a). Under such conditions, even intense rainfall is unlikely to raise the water table enough to induce landslides (Kim et al. 2004), although the response depends on the hydraulic properties of the subsurface. Instead, landslides are triggered due to the downward propagation of a wetting front from the ground surface into the subsurface amid rain infiltration. In this case, a significant amount of water can infiltrate and accumulate within the unsaturated zone during the storm, driven by soil anisotropy, heterogeneity, subsurface weathering profiles, and topographic influences (Zaslavsky and Sinai 1981). This decreases the soil matric suction, which provides an increased apparent strength and keeps the slope stable. If water flow continues, the generation of positive pore pressures might also occur at shallow depths that were previously within the vadose zone (Fig. 2b). Consequently, the mobilized shear strength of the ground decreases along the potential slip surface, ultimately triggering failure (Fourie et al. 1999, Aristizábal Giraldo et al. 2016). This mechanism was proposed based on observations of shallow landslides and debris flows initiating high on hillslopes, often just below the convex-to-concave slope transition, near ridge tops (Johnson and Sitar 1990). Top-down wetting-induced failure triggered by perched water table formation (Fig. 3): The initial conditions in this mechanism resemble those of the previous one, with a thick unsaturated zone exhibiting significant matric suction (Fig. 3a). A wetting front also propagates downward from the ground surface; however, in the presence of stronger shallow material, the positive pressures generated by the wetting front are insufficient to trigger shallow failures. Instead, the wetting front advances until it reaches deeper, lower-permeability layers, which slow or impede further

Study area and landslide‑triggering event The study area is a watershed located in Utuado, Puerto Rico (18° 15′ N, 66° 30′ W), the easternmost island of the Greater Antilles (Fig. 4a). Puerto Rico is mainly composed of deep layers of volcanic, intrusive, and sedimentary rocks dating from the Late Cretaceous Period (~100 to 66 Ma) to the Eocene Epoch (~56 to 34 Ma) (Silva- Tulla et al. 2018). Despite the steep slopes across the island, a few meters of saprolite as well as hillside soil overlie the bedrock due to in-place chemical weathering (Jibson 1989; Larsen and Torres- Sánchez 1992). Rainfall-induced landslides and debris flows are very common on the island due to the high frequency of intense

rainfall events (Bessette-Kirton et al. 2019), widespread distribution of weathered residual soils on hillslopes (Deere and Patton 1971), and changing land use practices (Larsen and Torres-Sánchez 1998). In fact, Puerto Rico has one of the highest hurricane frequencies in North America, with 85 hurricanes recorded between 1508 and 1997 (Neumann et al. 1987). Hurricane Maria struck the island on September 20, 2017, at 6:15 a.m. (Atlantic Standard Time) as a Category 4 hurricane, with maximum total rainfall values ranging from 733 (Ramos-Scharrón and Arima 2019) to 1029 mm (Keellings and Hernández Ayala 2019). The hurricane induced more than 70,000 landslides and debris flows, with most of them occurring on the same day (Hughes et al. 2019). Most landslides were shallow, translational, and triggered in soils or saprolite. Numerous landslides evolved into debris flows, eventually merging into down channels (Baum et al. 2023). The Utuado region in central Puerto Rico was severely affected, with a landslide area density exceeding 100 landslides/km2 (Hughes and Schulz 2020). The soil in Utuado is silty sand derived from the granodiorite-quartz diorite of the plutonic rocks of the Utuado batholith (Learned et al. 1981). On the other hand, Hurricane Maria was preceded by Hurricane Irma just 2 weeks earlier (September 6, 2017), and the resulting antecedent rainfall likely led to elevated water tables in hillslopes near valleybottom areas (Cangialosi et al. 2018), potentially causing bottom-up saturation-induced failures. The mean annual rainfall in Utuado ranges from 2000 to 3800 mm (Soil Survey Staff 2002; Lázaro and Fernández 2010). For this study, we considered the National Centers for Environmental Prediction (NCEP) Stage IV dataset (Du 2011) as most reliable, as it closely matched the partially available gauge data. Rainfall was recorded hourly at a spatial resolution of 0.2° by 0.2°, with a total of ~640 mm accumulated near the watershed by September 22, 2017, at 12:00 a.m. (Fig. 4b).

## Methods

CRISIS model CRISIS is a mechanistic model that couples a transient hydrological model of the user’s choice, here, ParFlow (Kollet and Maxwell 2008), with a seismic displacement model with a pseudo-3D slope stability approach (Gong et al. 2023). For this analysis, we focus on

rainfall-induced landslides only and do not incorporate the seismic component. The outputs of the model are 3D landslides with a welldefined location, geometry (area and volume), and timing of failure. By tracking how pore pressures develop and migrate within a slope up to failure, CRISIS can determine the specific failure mechanism that triggers each predicted landslide. Figure 5 outlines the CRISIS modeling workflow, which integrates two main components: a hydrological model (ParFlow) and a slope stability model. The sequence begins with a ParFlow spin-up run, initialized with a spatially uniform groundwater table across the study region. A constant recharge rate is applied over an extended period to allow the system to reach steady-state hydrological conditions (Module 1, Fig. 5). The resulting spatially variable water table is then used as the initial condition for the main simulation, providing a more realistic representation of complex groundwater conditions. In the main ParFlow run (Module 2, Fig. 5), pore pressure heads are computed for all cells and depths at each time step in response to the hurricane rainfall time series. These values are passed to an infinite slope stability analysis to identify potential triggering cells (Module 3, Fig. 5). Finally, 3D landslides are generated from the triggering cells at each time step using a pseudo-3D procedure (Module 4, Fig. 5).

Best‑estimate scenario relative to observed landslides (scenario 1) The model was first applied to the study area with near-realistic conditions to generate best-estimate landslide predictions relative to the observed failures shown in Fig. 4c. In this scenario, the subsurface consists of silty sand typical of Utuado, with saturated hydraulic conductivity (ks) decreasing gradually with depth. This depth-dependent decline in hydraulic conductivity is well-documented in empirical field and laboratory studies and has been incorporated into various hillslope and catchment hydrology models (Belcher et al. 2001; Ameli et al. 2016). To simplify the model, the saturated hydraulic conductivity (ks) was assumed to vary only with depth and remain spatially uniform. For shear strengths, an assumption of spatially uniform and constant shear strength results in unrealistic subsurface conditions and erroneous results. Thus, we implemented a simple correlation between slope and strength to generate spatially variable strength values for each 1-m cell across the watershed, capturing the

heterogeneity of the landscape. Steeper slopes were assigned higher shear strengths than gentler slopes, as gentler slopes often accumulate thicker colluvial deposits, which are generally weaker, whereas steep slopes tend to have thinner soil layers or even exposed bedrock, which are typically stronger. These values were primarily based on those reported by Baum and Lewis (2023) and were further refined through trial-and-error to better match the observed landslide occurrences. Results and discussion

Effect of geomorphic position This part of the analysis was based on the best-estimate scenario, in which shear strengths were varied both spatially and in depth (“Best-estimate scenario relative to observed landslides (scenario 1)” section). Figure 9a shows the initial water table depth estimated by the ParFlow spin-up run for this scenario. Figures 9b–g show the

predicted landslides (magenta polygons) at various time instants for this scenario. Failures are overlaid on a background depicting the flow accumulation area, a proxy for geomorphic position: high values correspond to lower positions (valley bottoms), while low values indicate higher positions (ridges). The mapped landslides are also included (black outlines) for reference. Each predicted landslide at each time instant was analyzed through pore pressure and factor-of-safety evolution to identify its failure mechanism. A bottom-up saturation-induced failure was first predicted on 19 September at 1:00 p.m. (Fig. 9c) due to a slight rise in the initially shallow groundwater table (Fig. 9a). Most susceptible slopes near valley bottoms (high flow accumulation areas) failed early (by 20 September, 11:00 a.m., 5 h after the hurricane’s onset) through similar bottom-up failures driven by the rising water table (Fig. 9e). Subsequently, the model predicted landslides occurring higher upslope (near ridge tops) triggered by top-down wetting-induced failures, where the initial water table was initially deeper (Fig. 9a). The dominant failure mechanism was notably affected by the slope’s geomorphic position. Bottom-up failures dominated slopes near valley bottoms (high flow accumulation areas) with shallow initial water tables (Fig. 9a). Ridge-top slopes, with deeper initial water tables under drier conditions, experienced top-down failures from wetting front propagation or perched water table formation. By 12:00 a.m. on September 22, 2017, the model predicted a cumulative landslide area density of approximately 8% (Fig. 9g), closely matching the mapped density of 5.5% (Fig. 4c). In terms of spatial distribution, the model generally performed well, accurately predicting landslides that overlapped, or were within a few meters of, the mapped locations, resulting in a relatively high true positive rate. Some overprediction occurred in areas that did not actually fail, but overall, the model captured the key patterns of landslide occurrence effectively. The minor overprediction and spatial mismatches can be attributed to both modeling and mapping limitations. Landslide mapping is typically performed after the event, so a single large, mapped landslide may represent several smaller, progressively triggered failures. In this

The model captured distinct failure mechanisms based on the slope geomorphic position: bottom-up saturation-induced failures predominated hillslopes near valley bottoms with initially shallow groundwater tables, whereas top-down wetting-induced failures prevailed near ridge tops where groundwater tables were initially deeper. Although no information was available regarding the specific failure mechanisms triggering each mapped landslide (Bayouth-Garcia and Hughes 2023), field observations in Utuado after Hurricane Maria documented numerous shallow ridge-top landslides that occurred in the absence of a shallow initial water table, indicating that many of these failures were likely top-down in nature (Silva-Tulla et al. 2018). Moreover, Hurricane Maria was preceded by Hurricane Irma just 2 weeks earlier (September 6, 2017). The rainfall from Irma likely raised water tables in some valleybottom areas (Cangialosi et al. 2018), which may have contributed to bottom-up failures. The geomorphic position also influenced the timing of failure. Bottom-up failures in valley bottoms occurred earlier than topdown failures and, in some cases, even prior to Hurricane Maria’s landfall. This reflects the fact that slopes underlain by shallow water tables were already close to instability and required only minimal additional rainfall to fail. Still, other factors, such as antecedent subsurface moisture and the temporal distribution of rainfall during the storm, can also influence failure timing. For example, under initially dry subsurface conditions, top-down failures could occur earlier than bottom-up failures, especially if triggered by short, high-intensity rainfall events. This analysis emphasizes the importance of hydrogeological modeling to capture the initial spatial variability of the groundwater table, a key feature of ParFlow. Models assuming an initially uniform water table fail to account for variations in groundwater table depth across the landscape, overlooking the influence of geomorphic position. Furthermore, accurately representing antecedent rainfall is vital, as it impacts the water table’s initial position and the thickness of the saturated and vadose zones. ParFlow addresses this through a constant recharge rate in its spin-up simulation: lower rates result in initially drier conditions, whereas higher rates represent wetter initial conditions. This analysis also highlights the importance of simulating three-dimensional groundwater flow, particularly in complex mountainous terrains such as Puerto Rico. Unlike vertical one-dimensional infiltration models, 3D flow

captures lateral subsurface movement, which is crucial for accurately representing water redistribution. This prevents the overestimation of drainage at ridge-tops and the underestimation of water accumulation near valley bottoms.

Effect of material cohesion

After evaluating the best-estimate simulation against the observed landslides, analyses were conducted to assess the impact of material cohesion, which controls the strength of the shallow subsurface, on dominant failure mechanisms. For this analysis, shear strengths were held constant (spatially and with depth) within each scenario, but cohesion varied between scenarios: c′ = 5 kPa (scenario 3), 20 kPa (scenario 2), and 25 kPa (scenario 4). Figure 12 shows the predicted total cumulative landslide area density (black curves) over time for the three different cohesions, with contributions from three failure mechanisms. The total cumulative landslide area density increased as cohesion decreased, with predictions of 0% for c′ = 25 kPa, 32% for c′ = 20 kPa, and 91% for c′ = 5 kPa. Lower cohesion reduces shear strength relative to the rainfall-induced pore water pressures, leading to a lower FS and higher failure susceptibility, especially at shallower subsurface layers. The significantly high predicted landslide area densities can be largely attributed to the assumption of geospatially constant shear strengths, which do not account for landscape complexities. In this part of the analysis, the goal is not to replicate observed failures (as in the best-estimate scenario), but rather to theoretically understand the impact of subsurface properties, which may vary across the landscape. For c′ = 20 kPa, some bottom-up saturation-induced failures (2.5% cumulative landslide area density) were predicted before the hurricane’s onset, between 19 September, 10:00 p.m., and 20 September, 5:00 a.m. Subsequently, on 20 September, at 6:00 a.m., exclusively top-down failures triggered by the formation of a perched water table started to occur with a cumulative landslide area density of 29.5%. By 21 September, 8:00 a.m., no further landslides were predicted. The high cohesions prevented any top-down failures due to wetting front propagation. Even if a wetting front formed and propagated downward, the higher cohesion prevented shallow failures. Consequently, the wetting front reached deeper, less permeable layers, and a perched water table was formed (Fig. 11b), triggering deeper failures (Fig. 11c). For c′ = 5 kPa, 61% of the study area failed initially on September 19, 12:00 a.m., with all failures triggered by the bottomup saturation mechanism. These failures occurred on slopes with inclinations exceeding the friction angle ( 휙′ = 37°), driven by slope geometry rather than hurricane-induced pore pressures. This erroneous result is due to the assumption of spatially constant and low shear strengths across the topography, which fails to account for the landscape’s complexities. The percentage of bottom-up failures slightly increased to 64% by September 20 at 4:00 a.m. After this point, landslides were exclusively induced by top-down wettinginduced mechanisms, with 16% triggered by a perched water table and 11% by the wetting front. Effect of subsurface material type

The subsurface material type, characterized by both shear strengths and hydraulic conductivity, greatly influenced the failure mechanisms, the timing of landslides, and the total landslide area density. Figure 15 shows the total cumulative landslide area density (black curves) over time for clay (scenario 5), silt (scenario 6), and sand (scenario 7), with contributions from three failure mechanisms. Clays did not trigger any failures for this rainfall event because their low hydraulic conductivity largely impeded water infiltration (Fig. 15a). The high rainfall intensities exceeded the surface infiltration capacity, causing water to run off rather than infiltrate,

which limited pore pressure buildup and prevented slope failures. Silts, in contrast, led to both bottom-up saturation-induced failures (25% landslide area density between 19 September, 2:00 p.m., and 20 September, 5:00 a.m.) and top-down failures driven by perched water tables (51% landslide area density), resulting in a total landslide area density of 76%. However, failures due to the wetting front were not triggered because of the high cohesion, inhibiting shallow failures. On the other hand, sands exclusively triggered bottom-up saturation-induced failures, even on slopes located near ridge tops, starting on 19 September at 11:00 p.m. (Fig. 15c). The high hydraulic conductivity of sand allowed rapid water infiltration, quickly reaching the groundwater table and causing it to rise and subsequently trigger failures (Fig. 16). Although hydraulic conductivity was set to decrease gradually within the 2 m-thick domain, it remained sufficiently high throughout to permit rapid drainage. This prevented the development of a distinct wetting front, as water could not be retained within the highly permeable layers. Likewise, perched water tables did not form due to this high infiltration capacity. Moreover, sand facilitated rapid pore pressure buildup, triggering failures starting 7 h before the hurricane and occurring abruptly over a short span of 9 h. It is important to highlight that this analysis assumed the same subsurface material type across all slopes (per scenario), whereas in real landscapes, subsurface materials typically vary spatially and in depth. Subsurface materials vary with depth due to factors such as weathering profiles and slope steepness, which influence soil thickness on hillsides as well as saprolite and bedrock exposure. Thus, accurate mapping and testing are crucial to understanding the spatial and depth variations in subsurface properties. This prevented the modeling of hydraulic recharge zones that allow water to infiltrate the subsurface at slopes where bedrock is shallow or even exposed and subsequently flows to adjacent slopes with thicker soil layers that limit water infiltration. Hence, this prevented the prediction of failures caused by water exfiltration from bedrock, a common real-world issue (Johnson and Sitar 1990). To address this limitation, future research should incorporate spatial variability in soil thickness based on topographic factors such as slope inclination. •	 Model simplifications and bias In this analysis, the influence of each factor on the landslide failure mechanism was examined separately, but studying the combined impact of these factors on failure mechanisms across the topography is also crucial. Therefore, accurate, high-resolution studies are needed to capture the spatial and depth-specific distributions of the area’s geology, topography, hydraulic properties, geomorphology, weathering profiles, bedrock characteristics, and shear strengths to allow a comprehensive study accounting for all these variations. Additionally, this analysis was applied to a relatively small watershed, which highlights the need for its application to more case histories for validation and refinement. The analysis was also conducted within a 2-m-thick domain, assuming a no-flow bottom boundary. This setup may bias results toward the formation of a perched water table rather than a rise in the groundwater table. Exploring alternative boundary conditions and possibly using thicker domains, despite the limitations of the infinite slope stability model for deeper analyses, could provide more realistic insights. •	 Rainfall time series characteristics Other important factors, such as the rainfall time series, were not considered in our analysis. The focus of this study was specifically on the rainfall patterns observed during Hurricane Maria in Utuado, an extreme weather event. However, rainfall intensity and duration, which can vary from short, intense storms to prolonged, moderate precipitation, are likely to significantly influence failure mechanisms. Therefore, future research should prioritize investigating how different rainfall time series interact with subsurface hydraulic properties to better understand their combined impact on dominant failure processes. •	 Mapped landslide inventories High-quality mapped landslide inventories offer valuable data for validating model results. However, compiling these inventories is challenging, and methodological biases can influ-

Most existing inventories document landslide locations and areas, and rarely their volumes, but to our knowledge, none provide information on the failure mechanism for each individual landslide. As a result, validation of analyses like this one often depends on reported failure mechanisms from a limited set of representative landslides.

Summary and conclusions A regional predictive model for rainfall-induced landslides (CRISIS), which couples ParFlow with a pseudo-3D slope stability approach, was developed and introduced in this study. CRISIS was applied to a watershed in Utuado, Puerto Rico, impacted by Hurricane Maria in 2017. Initially, the model was run with near-realistic conditions to generate best-estimate predictions relative to the observed landslides. Subsequently, a series of hypothetical scenarios with altered subsurface properties was simulated to explore the factors that govern the occurrence of different failure mechanisms. Key factors analyzed included geomorphic position, initial hydrological conditions, subsurface cohesion, and subsurface material types. In addition to the commonly considered bottom-up saturation-induced failure caused by a rising groundwater table, this study also examined top-down wetting-induced mechanisms, including failure from a downward-propagating wetting front or the formation of a perched water table above less permeable material. The conclusions from this study can be summarized as follows:

•	 For the best-estimate scenario with spatially variable shear strengths, the model reasonably reproduced the mapped landslides in terms of both spatial distribution and watershed-scale landslide area density. Further refinement of the geospatial shear strength distribution is expected to yield additional improvements in performance. •	 Diverse failure mechanisms can be triggered across the topography depending on a combination of factors, including the hillslope’s geomorphic position, the subsurface shear strength and hydraulic properties, and initial hydrological conditions. •	 The slope’s geomorphic position greatly influenced the spatial distribution of the initial groundwater table level. This resulted in the triggering of different failure mechanisms across the topography: bottom-up saturation-induced failures near valley bottoms, where the initial groundwater table is typically shallow, and top-down wetting-induced failures near ridge-tops, where the initial groundwater table tends to be deeper. This highlights the importance of hydrogeological modeling in regional-scale simulations, as opposed to assuming a uniform initial groundwater table depth, as is common in many existing models. It also highlights the necessity of simulating three-dimensional groundwater flow as opposed to only vertical one-dimensional infiltration, particularly in complex mountainous regions like Puerto Rico. •	 Cohesion played a key role in determining the dominant failure mechanism as well as the landslide thickness, as indicated by the analyzed scenarios. High cohesion strengthened the shallow subsurface layers, preventing failures via the downward propagation of a wetting front. As a result, water accumulated above deeper layers with lower hydraulic
